messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi Mensah is a 33-year-old Ghanaian-American man, married and currently employed as a social media manager for a mid-sized nonprofit organization. He was referred for psychological assessment following a period of sustained occupational difficulty and what his wife described, in a brief note accompanying the referral, as him "not being the same person who came back." Kofi presents with a PCL-5 score of 68, consistent with severe posttraumatic stress, and has been reluctant to seek help until now, having spent the better part of eighteen months persuading himself that what he experienced was simply part of the job.

Approximately two years ago, Kofi was deployed as a logistics coordinator for a humanitarian relief organization operating in a conflict zone in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. He had done similar work before — shorter stints, more stable regions — and had considered himself experienced enough to manage whatever he encountered. What he was not prepared for was a morning in early spring when a supply convoy he had personally organized and dispatched was ambushed on a road he had cleared through standard protocol. Three local colleagues were killed. Kofi was at the distribution point when the radio call came in. He heard the voices, heard the chaos, and then heard nothing. He was the one who had approved the route. He was the one who had signed off on the departure time. In the weeks that followed, he moved through the remaining deployment in a kind of functional dissociation, completing tasks, filing reports, and saying very little to anyone about what he carried.

Since returning to the United States and resuming work, Kofi has found that the ordinary rhythms of his job have become unexpectedly treacherous. His role requires him to monitor multiple content streams simultaneously, tracking breaking news, conflict updates, and humanitarian crises across social platforms in real time. The scrolling feeds — the sudden appearance of images from active war zones, the audio clips embedded in news posts, the ambient noise of urgency that defines his screen — place him in a sustained state of alertness that does not resolve when he closes his laptop. He sits at his desk with his back to the wall when he can arrange it, and colleagues have noticed that he flinches visibly when someone approaches him from behind or when a phone alarm sounds unexpectedly nearby. He has difficulty sustaining concentration on single tasks, often re-reading the same paragraph of a content brief several times without retaining it, which he has begun to attribute to some fundamental deterioration in his cognitive capacity.

What frightens Kofi most is not the external world but his own internal one. He had come to believe, with a quiet and absolute certainty, that he cannot trust his own judgment — that the man who approved that route, who followed protocol and still got people killed, is the man he still is. He does not experience this as guilt in any simple sense; it is more like a structural conclusion about his reliability as a person. When memories of that morning surface, he pushes them away deliberately, holding them at a distance through a practiced detachment that he describes as "going somewhere else for a second." He does not allow himself to think through the events in any sustained way, and has told his wife only the barest outline of what happened.

Alongside this sits something harder and more outward-facing: Kofi is consumed by the knowledge that nothing has been done. The men responsible for the ambush have faced no accountability. The organization conducted an internal review and issued no findings. He had come to understand his own suffering as not merely personal but as evidence of a profound injustice that the world had simply absorbed and moved on from, and this understanding has made it difficult for him to invest in anything that feels like recovery. Why heal, some part of him seems to ask, when the record has not been corrected?

What finally brought him to seek help was his wife telling him, quietly and without accusation, that she felt like she was living with someone who was always about to leave. Kofi does not know exactly what he is hoping for. He knows only that he is exhausted by the vigilance, and that he would like, at minimum, to be able to sit at his desk without feeling that something is still coming.
